REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
Serial bomb blasts In Varanasi on the 7th March, 2006 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, it is with utmost grief and sorrow that I 
refer to the dastardly terrorist strike on the 7th March, 2006 on the ancient Sankat Mochan 
Temple in the holy city of Varanasi and the Cantonment Railway Station, Varanasi reportedly 
killing about 20 people and injuring several others. 
No words are strong enough to condemn this heinous act. The killing of so many 
innocent persons has shocked the entire nation. I am sure that the whole House will join me in 
condemning this cowardly and senseless act, and in offering condolences to the bereaved families, 
and pray for early recovery of those who got injured in these blasts. 
On this occasion, we express our firm resolve to fight terrorism with determination. 
Such outrageous acts of terrorism are intended to test our patience and secular credentials. We 
appeal to all sections of the society to rise to the occasion and maintain perfect peace and calm in 
order to face the challenge posed by this mindless act of terrorism. 
I request Members to rise in their piaces and observe silence as a mark of respect to the 
memory of those who lost their lives in this tragedy. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

*241. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state:

Hoax call regarding bomb in Parliament House 
†*242. SHRI VASANT CHAVAN: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether an E-mail was received with regard to the rumour of a bomb 
planted in the Parliament House; 
(b) if so, whether accused have been caught; and 
(c) the details of the terrorist organization working behind the said 
rumour/E-mail? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir.  An e-mail was received on 16th 
December, 2005 at the Central Mail Box of U.S. Embassy, New Delhi to the 
effect that there would be a bomb blast in the Parliament and Consulates of 
United States in India at 1146 hrs on 16.12.2005. 
(b) No, Sir. 
(c) The investigation into the case conducted so far has revealed that the 
e-mail was sent from an internet  face called "Broadband Net Cafe", 
Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, by an unknown person. No terrorist organisation, 
which could be behind sending the e-mail, has so far been identified nor has any 
claimed the responsibility. Investigation in to the case registered vide FIR No. 
150/05 on 16.12.2005 by the Special Cell of Delhi Police is continuing.

Non-deposit of employer's EPF share by contractors 
*246. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of contractors do not deposit 
regularly/properly the employer's share of EPF contribution and as a result 
thereof, workers are unable to get the benefits of their EPF contributions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the number of defaulting 
contractors and the number of the aff ected contract workers in each State; 
and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRA SEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) As the Schemes framed under the 
Employees' Provident funds & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 do not 
distinguish an employee employed by an employer either directly or through a 
contractor, nor separate data in respect of contractors is maintained by the 
Employees' Provident Fund Organization. However, all employees, whether 
employed by an employer directly or through a contractor in connection with 
the work of a covered establishment, are entitled to beco me members of the 
employees' Provident Fund and to avail benefits thereof. The total oustanding 
dues of all the establishements (including contractors), as on 31.03.2005, are Rs. 
2144.82 crore. 
(c) wherever default in respect of such employees is noticed, action in 
accordance with provisions of the Act are taken. This includes assessment of 
dues under section 7A and recovery thereof by way of prosecution under 
section 14, filing of complaints under section 406/409 of IPC, attachment of 
movable/immovable property and arrest of defaulters. 
Uniform Labour Policy 
†*247. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
(a) whether it is fact that the country needs a uniform labour policy 
acceptable to all; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that different labour laws have been 
implemented by different departments in the name of labour reforms; and 
(d) if so, the details of such departments indicating the variation in 
labour laws applicable therein? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRA SEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) The Ministry of Labour and 
Employment is mandated to create a work environment conducive to 
achieving a high rate of economic growth with due regard to protecting and 
safeguarding the interests of the workers.  The Ministry seeks to achieve this 
objective through implementation of an array of labour legislations. India's 
labour policy is mainly based on labour laws. The Ministry has always been 
committed to the ethos and culture of tripartism. The Ministry continues to have 
consultation with the social partners to obtain a consensus for enacting new 
laws or bringing about changes in the existing laws. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE:

state: 
(a) the present status of the Unorga nised Sector Worker's Social 
Security Scheme launched-by his Ministry during 2004; 
(b) how many members have been enrolled under the said scheme and the 
amount of contributions realized; and 
(c) how much expenditure has incurred so far for implementing the said 
scheme? 
8 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRA SEKHAR RAO): (a) The Unor ganised Sector Workers Social 
Security Scheme, 2004 launched in January 2004 on pilot basis in fifty 
districts of the country has since been closed.

Rs. 17.5 lakh was collected as contribution. 
(c) The contributions received from workers under the scheme have been 
utilised towards making premium paym ents under the Universal Health 
Insurance Scheme (UHIS) and personal  accident insurance scheme for the

Abolition of child labour 
*249. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
SHRIMATI KAMLA MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are contemplating to abolish child labour in the 
country within a time bound programme; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have received any financial aid from the World 
Bank, International Labour Organisation and UNICEF for abolition of child 
labour; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and to what extent these financial aids are 
found to be helpful in achieving the goal? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRA SEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) Government is committed to the goal 
of eradication of child labour in all its forms beginning with children working 
in hazardous occupations/processes. In this direction, Government is 
implementing the scheme of National Child Labour Projects (NCLPs) in 250 
districts of 21 states in the country. Under the scheme children withdrawn 
from work are put into the Special Schools where these children are provided 
basis education, vocational training,

Attack on NMDC, Hiroli (Chhattisgarh) by Maoists 
†*251. SHRI LAXMINARAYAN SHARMA: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that maoists had killed many personnel of CISF 
and looted weapons on the 7th February, 2006 by attacking a PSU, National 
Mineral Development Corporation, Hiroli (Chhattisgarh); and 
(b) if so, the details of the measures being taken by Government for 
security of this area in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) On 9.2.2006, the naxalites attacked the 
National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC) magazine at Hiroli in 
Chhattisgarh and killed 8 CISF personnel and took away 14 SLRs and a large 
quantity of explosives from the magazine.

requisite help for intensive search and combing operations in the area. DG, 
CISF has been asked to conduct a security survey of all the magazines manned 
by them in the naxal affected areas and take steps to strengthen their security 
wherever required. Besides, the naxal af fected States have been advised to 
enhance the security of magazines and strictly enforce regulations on 
manufacture, movement and storage of explosives.

1629. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

Eastern region as an important Economic link with the BIMSTEC members, 
in anticipation that the North Eastern States could become India's link to

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMME RCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) BIST-EC (Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka and 
Thailand-Economic Cooperation), a sub-regional economic grouping was formed 
in Bangkok in June 1997. Subsequently Myanmar (December 1997), Bhutan and 
Nepal (February 2004) joined the forum. It was decided at the First BIMSTEC 
summit held in Bangkok on July 30-31, 2004 to rename BIMSTE-EC as

Technical and Economic Cooperation". BIMSTEC has identified the areas of 
cooperation in the sectors of Transport and Communication, Tourism, Trade and 
Investment, Fisheries, Technology, Energy, Agriculture, Public Health, 
Poverty Alleviation, Counter Terroris m and Transnational Crimes, Cultural 
Cooperation, Environment and Disaster Management and People to People 
Contacts. Many of these sectors will ultimately lead to further strengthening of 
India's economic links with other member countries of BIMSTEC. Bangladesh, 
Bhutan and Myanmar, which are members of BIMSTEC, are in the vicinity of the 
North Eastern States of India making them beneficiaries of any economic 
links which would ultimately develop with in BIMSTEC. In addition, a 
Framework Agreement for establishing BIMSTEC Free Trade Area (FTA) was 
signed in February 2004. This will also provide opportunity to the North Eastern 
States to enhance various economic activities leading to overall progress of the 
region.

WTO Ministerial meet in Hong Kong 
1642. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether a World Trade Organization (WTO) Ministerial meet was 
held in Hong Kong in December last; 
(b) if so, the issues discussed and decisions taken therein; and 
(c) whether any policy guidelines were adopted to protect the interest of the 
farmers in small and developing countries against the protectionist subsidies 
granted by developed countries for promoting their farmers' interests? 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) Yes.  Sir. The Sixth WTO Ministerial 
Conference was held from 13-18 December, 2005 at Hong Kong. This 
Ministerial Conference discussed among other issues, issues relating to 
reduction of domestic supports, elimin ation of export subsidies, sensitive 
products, special products and special safeguard mechanism in agriculture; 
elimination of export subsidies and accelerated reduction of domestic support 
in cotton; non-agricultural market access; services; development package for 
least developed countries and other development issues under the Doha Work 
Programme. 
The decisions taken at the Minister ial Conference are reflected in the 
Ministerial Declaration adopted by the Ministers on 18th December, 2005. 
Copies of the Ministerial Declaration have been placed in the Parliament 
Library. 
(c) The Hong Kong Ministerial Conference resolved that there would be 
effective cuts in trade distorting domestic support consistent with the July 
Framework Agreement of the WTO adopted on 1st August, 2004. Further, it 
was resolved that parallel elimination of all forms of export subsidies and 
disciplines on all export measures with equivalent effect would be completed 
by the end of 2013, with a substantial part being eliminated half-way 
through. The developing countries will have the flexibility to self-designate an 
appropriate number of tariff lines as Special Products guided by indicators 
based on the criteria of food security, livelihood security and rural 
development. Developing country members will also have the right to have 
recourse to a Special Safeguard Mechanism based on import quantity and price 
triggers, with precise arrangements to be further defined to protect them against 
surge in imports or sudden decline in prices of agriculture commodities.

Sustainable livelihood for small farmers 
1646. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: W ill the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any representation was recei ved from the group of farmers 
who took part in a parallel "peoples camp" in Hong Kong during the recent 
WTO Ministerial meeting seeking Government's intervention to protect 
sustainable livelihood for small farmers in the context of the WTO 
negotiations; 
(b) if so, the nature and extent of protection sought for small farmers; and 
(c) what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) A number of representations were received 
from group of farmers and NGOs in connection with the Hong Kong 
Ministerial in December, 2005. 
Essentially they emphasized that agriculture is a major source of 
livelihood for Indian farmers and their interests should be protected from the 
unfair agriculture trade practices adopted by developed countries, 
48 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
which could compound the woes of Indian farmers. They advocated adequate 
protection to safeguard the interests of the Indian farmers. 
(c) Government is fully aware of the concerns of Indian farmers and 
accordingly took a strong and princi pled stand during the Hong Kong 
Ministerial to safeguard their interests. India took a conscious position that the 
developing countries cannot be asked to reduce their agriculture tariffs as long as 
the developed countries c ontinue to subsidize the domestic produce of their 
farmers and also extend export subsidies to them. 
The issue was also collectively raised with like-minded countries that 
form the G-20 and G-33 Group. Consequently, the Hong Kong Ministerial 
Declaration recognized the right of developing countries to self-designate an 
appropriate number of tariff lines as Special Products with a view to ensuring 
their food security, livelihood security and rural development needs. On these 
lines, zero or a minimal tariff reduction would be undertaken. Developing 
country members will also have a right to take recourse to a Special Safeguard 
Mechanism to guard against surge in volume of imports and also against price 
depressions. 
Also, developing countries like India, with no commitments on 
reduction of aggregate measure of support, would be exempted from 
reduction in their-de-minimis support and in overall trade distorting support. 
Furthermore, the developing country members will also be able to continue to 
benefit from the provisions of providing subsidies on transport and marketing 
of their agriculture exports till 2018. 
The negotiations are proceeding with a view to establish modalities in 
agriculture by 30 April, 2006, with draft Schedules to be submitted by July 
31,2006, under an overall resolve by WTO Ministers at Hong Kong to 
complete the Doha Work Programme fully and conclude negotiations in 2006. 
The Government has been holding stakeholder consultations to protect 
and pursue our national interest, in particular the interests of our farmers. 
Government is committed to interv ene in a WTO- compatible manner, 
including by calibrating the applied tariffs within the bound duties, to protect their 
interests. 
To protect the interests of farmers the Government has also put in place a 
suitable mechanism for monitoring the imports of sensitive items 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
and are committed to providing adequate protection to domestic producers through 
WTO compatible measures.

Strategies adopted at Valetta, Malta to protect farmers' interests 
1653. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of the fact that in most of the developing 
Commonwealth countries including India over 60 per cent of the people depend 
on agriculture for their livelihood, a strategy was evolved at the recent meeting 
of the Commonwealth countries at Valetta in Malta, to provide for livelihood 
security for the farmers by removing distortions in international trade rules 
under WTO regime, which are created by developed countries through huge 
domestic support and export subsidies to protect their farmers; 
54 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details of such strategy; and 
(c) the steps taken and being taken by Government in the light of the 
strategy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) The Commonwealth Heads of Government 
Meeting (CHOGM) was held in Valetta, Malta on 25-27 November, 2005. In 
the "Valetta Statement on Multilateral Trade" issued at the conclusion of the 
Summit, the Heads of States, inter-alia, recognized the following:— 
"We are mindful of the critical importance of agriculture to 
developing economies for subsistence, as a reservoir of future economic 
growth, and as a sector where many of our members have a potential 
comparative advantage. Agriculture is the most distorted sector of world 
trade and we are determined to pursue significant progress towards fuller 
and more meaningful subjection of agricultural production and trade to 
multilateral disciplines. We note the offer on agriculture made by the 
United States of America and express the hope that the European Union 
and others who maintain high levels of agricultural protection respond in 
the same spirit." 
(c) India's overall objectives in the negotiations launched at the Doha 
Ministerial Conference of the WTO in November, 2001 have been to secure a 
final outcome on agriculture that is consistent with the agreed negotiating 
mandate for early elimination of all forms of export subsidies, substantial and 
effective reductions in trade-distor ting domestic support, and substantial 
improvements in market access particularly for products of export interest to 
developing countries. Simultaneously, it has been agreed that special and 
differential treatment for developing coun tries will be integral to all aspects 
of the negotiations, recognizing that agriculture is of critical importance to 
the economic development of developing country members and they must be 
able to pursue agricultural policies that are supportive of their development goals, 
poverty reduction strategies, food security and livelihood concerns. 
The Hong Kong Ministerial Declaration also included a decision to 
eliminate export subsidies, which are mainly provided by some developed 
countries, by 2013, with substantial part in the first half of implementation period 
and to eliminate cotton export subsidies by developed countries 
55 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
by 2006. Developing countries will continue to benefit from the provisions on 
marketing and transport subsidies on agricultural exports for five years after the 
end date for elimination of all forms of export subsidies. On trade-distorting 
domestic support, the three heaviest subsidizers will attract the steepest cuts also in 
the reductions in their AMS, while the developing countries without agricultural 
market subsidy will be exempt from any cuts on de minimis and on overall 
trade-distorting support levels. In respect of market access commitments, it has 
been agreed that a four-band tariff reduction formula will be developed. In 
order to address their food security, livelihood and rural development needs, 
developing countries to have the flexibility to self-designate an appropriate 
number of Special Products, whose treatment will be more flexible. In order 
to safeguard farmers in developing countries against import surges and adverse 
global price movements, import quantity and price triggers have been agreed 
as the core structural elements of the Special Safeguard Mechanism.

work in areas such as forensics and case management at court level in a bid to restore the

Recruitment of sSurrendered militants in Para-Military Forces 
1729. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is true that the surrendered militants of the erstwhile 
Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) have been recruited by the CRPF and Assam 
Rifles as a step in conformity with the peace accord;

of law and order, protection of country's sovereignty and particularly how far 
their instinct could permit for counter insurgency operations;

forces?

Settlement (MoS), it was decided to recruit a maximum of 1000 surrendered

surrendered militants shall be recruited, who fulfil the eligibility condition for 
recruitment of to the post of constable/follower and who qualify through the 
prescribed normal selection procedure. Also only such surrendered militants are

through a Screening Committee.

reported.

of participation in the security of the country. 
Enquiry into Delhi bomb blasts 
†1730. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the enquiry into Delh i bomb blasts case has been 
completed; 
(b) if so, the outfit, found guilty for this incident; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
128 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the action taken so far against the culprits? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) to (c) Five major incidents of bomb blasts had 
taken place in Delhi during the year 2005.  The first two explosions occurred 
on 22nd May, 2005 in Liberty Cinema and Satyam Cinema. Investigation into 
these two cases has been completed and chargesheet has been filed in the court 
against eight accused persons. The cases are pending trial. Interrogation of 
accused persons has revealed that they are members of the banned terrorist 
organisation Babbar Khalsa International. 
There were three bomb explosions on 29th October, 2005-one each at 
Paharganj, Sarojini Nagar Market and Kalkaji. Investigation into the cases 
registered in connection with explosi ons at Paharganj and Kalkaji is still 
continuing. The investigation into the case relating to Sarojini Nagar Market has 
been completed and chargesheet has been filed against three accused persons in 
the court and the case is pending trial. The fourth accused, wanted in 
connection with the serial blasts, was killed in an encounter on 16.1.2006 in 
Jammu and Kashmir. It has been revealed during investigation that the blasts 
were the handiwork of militant organisation Lashkar-e-Tayyeba (LeT).

Commission for protection of children 
†1746. SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to set up a commission for 
protection of children from atrocities; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Commission for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 notified as 
Act No. 4 of 2006 in the Gazette of India, Extra Ordinary Part-ll, Section-I on 
20th January, 2006. The Act envisages setting up a National Commission at the 
National level and the State Commissions at the State level for Protection of 
Child Rights. Some of the main features of the Commission are given below: 
• The Commission to examine and review the safeguards 
provided by Constitution or any law for the protection of child 
rights and recommend measures for their effective 
implementation. 
• The Commission to examine all factors that inhibit the 
enjoyment of rights of most vulnerable children and children in 
need of special care and protection. 
• The Commission to study treaties and other international 
instruments and undertake periodical review of existing 
policies, programmes and other activities on child rights and make 
recommendation for their effect ive implementation in the best 
interest of children. 
• The Commission will inquire into complaints and take suo motu 
notice of matter relating to deprivation of child rights, non-
implementation of laws for protection and development of 
children and non-compliance of policy decision, guidelines or and 
to provide relief to such children.

• Any other functions as it may consider necessary for the 
promotion of child rights. 
• The Commission may summon and enforce the attendance of any 
person and examine him on oath. 
• Recommending to the concerned Government or authority the 
initiation of proceedings for prosecution or such other action as 
deem fit against the concerned person(s). 
• Recommending to the concerned Government or authority for the 
grant of such interim relief to the victim or the members of his 
family as the Commission consider necessary.

†1755. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

been assessed with regard to farmers families in rural areas whereas their average 
income is Just Rs. 2115/- p.m.;

expenditure is rising since last few years; and

2001-02 and 2005?

DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) 
According to NSS 59th round Survey on 'Situation Assessment Survey of 
Farmers' conducted in Jan—December, 2003, the average per capita 
expenditure on farmer household is Rs. 502.83. Taking the average 
household size as 5.5, the average monthly consumption expenditure of a farmer 
household is Rs. 2765.57 at national level. (Report No. 495 (59/ 33/4). The result

business and non farm business per farmer household as Rs. 2115/per month at 
all-India Level (Report No. 497(59/33/5). However, this figure excludes 
income from rent, dividend, interest and remittances.

average monthly consumption expenditure and monthly income of farmer

Rural habitations without proper drinking water 
1759. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of rural habitations in the country that remain without 
proper drinking water facility, State-wise; 
(b) the time-schedule chalked out to provide drinking water to all these 
rural habitations, State-wise; 
(c) the number of rural habitations provided with central assistance/ 
through central schemes during each of the last two years, State-wise; and 
(d) the reasons for not achieving the targets, if any? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) As per the Comprehensive 
Action Plan, 1999 and the subsequent coverage status reported by States/ Union 
Territories till 31.1.2006, there are 47, 476 habitations not fully covered with 
drinking water supply (3,891 Not covered and 43,585 Partially Covered). The 
State-wise list is given in the Stat ement (See below). However, since the 
coverage status is a dynamic one due to various factors like increase is 
population, sources going dry, emergence of water quality problems, failure in 
source and system etc., the Fully Covered habitations sometimes slip back to 
Partially Covered or Not Covered category. 
(b) Bharat Nirman has been conceived as a plan to build rural 
infrastructure in four years period (2005-06 to 2008-09). Rural drinking water 
is one of the components of Bharat Nirman. Under the said com ponent, it is 
envisaged to cover all uncovered habitations and also to address the problem of 
slippage and water quality. 
(c) and (d) Rural drinking water is a State subject, and State 
Governments responsible to provide drinking water facilities in rural 
habitations. The Central Government, however, supplements the efforts of State 
Governments in this regard by renderi ng financial assistance to the States 
through a Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP). The assistance is not provided 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
direct to the rural habitations. The St ate Governments are competent to plan, 
sanction, implement and execute rural water supply projects from the Central 
funds. With the assistance provided, the State Governments could cover 54,890 
habitation, which include uncovered, slipped back and quality affected 
habitations till 31.1.2006 against the target of coverage of 56270 habitations 
during 2005-06.

Committee to review the poverty alleviation programmes 
1761. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR:  Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to constitute a committee 
to review the poverty alleviation programmes being implemented by 
different States in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have chalked out any plan to eradicate poverty 
and rural unemployment within a period often years; and 
170 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the steps being taken by Government for effective 
implementation of these schemes/programmes meant for the purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) The 
Ministry of Rural Development has already a Performance Review 
Committee to review all the rural development programmes including 
poverty alleviation programmes being implemented by the State 
Governments/LIT Administrations. 
(c) The Tenth Plan envisages creation of 50 million employment 
opportunities during 2002-07. To create employment potential the Tenth 
Five Year Plan has identified labour intensive sector and sub sectors for 
development such as agriculture, in cluding social forestry, animal 
husbandry, fishing, horticulture and related areas and small and medium 
industries, construction, tourism, information technology, financial sector, 
education and health. At the all Indi a level, the Tenth Five Year Plan 
document has projected that the proportion of people living below poverty 
line is expected to decline to 19.3 percentage by 2006-07, as compared 
to 26.1 percentage in 1999-2000. 
Employment Generation is a multi-sectoral issue involving several 
Ministries/Sectors. The Ministry of Rural Development is implementing three 
major employment generation schemes namely, Swarnjayanti Gram Swarojgar 
Yojana (SGSY) for self employment, Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana 
(SGRY) and National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP) as wage 
employment programmes. The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 
(NREGA) has come into force w.e.f. 2nd February 2006 in the identified 200 
most backward districts to provide legal guarantee of 100 days of unskilled 
manual work to each rural household demanding for it in a financial year. 
(d) The Ministry of Rural Development places special emphasis on 
monitoring and evaluation of its programmes. The important instruments 
of monitoring mechanism include Review by Union Ministers, Meetings 
of Performance Review Committee, Area Officer's Scheme, Field Visits, 
Monitoring of Release of Funds, Analysis of Periodical Progress Reports, 
Receipt of Audit Reports and Utilisation Certificates, Monitoring by National 
Level Monitors (NLMs) and District Level Monitors (DLMs), Concurrent 
and Quick Evaluation Studies and Impact Assessment Studies. The State 
Governments have been advised to adhere to multi pronged strategy 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
including awareness about the Rural Development Schemes at grass root level, 
transparency, accountability and social audit by the Gram Panchayat to 
provide benefits of the rural development programmes to target groups.

(a) whether Central Government provides funds to the States for potable

(b) if so, the number of habitations covered so far and likely to be 
covered under the said programme along with the amount to be spent therein 
and the time limit fixed for the same, in the State of Rajasthan; 
(c) the status and achievement made under the said programme in 
Rajasthan; 
 
(d) in above context, wh ether there is any proposal from the 
Government of Rajasthan is pending for consideration with the Centre; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and timeframe for its disposal?

Conference of Union and State Ministers regarding drinking water 
in rural areas 
1764. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any conference of Union and State Ministers was held to 
discuss about drinking water in rural areas; 
(b) if so, the details of issues discussed; 
(c) the recommendations made and the action proposed to be taken; 
(d) whether drinking water is to be provided to all the villages under the 
Bharat Nirman Programme; 
(e) if so, the details thereof including investment to be made; and 
(f) the targets fixed and achievements made so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) A Conference of State 
Ministers in charge of rural drinking water supply and sanitation was held on 
31st January-1st February 2006 in New Delhi. The Conference was 
inaugurated by the Prime Minister and it was attended by State Ministers in-
charge of rural drinking water and sanitation and officers of Central and State 
Governments. 
(b) and (c) The issues discussed du ring the Conference were— review 
of the progress made in the current year under Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP), Swajaldhara and Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC), 
increasing the role of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) 
174 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
in decentralized service delivery and system sustainability, strategy for 
effective implementation of the drinking water component of Bharat 
Nirman, promotion of source strengthening measures, integrated approach to 
tackling water quality problems, water quality monitoring and surveillance and 
policy and implementation issues pertaining to TSC including creation of 
awareness and social mobilization. 
The following resolutions were adopted during the Conference: 
• Work towards achieving the goals set under Bharat Nirman, i.e., 
provision of at least 40 litres per capita per day (Ipcd) of safe 
drinking water to all habitations, in a time bound manner, in the next 
four years; 
• Cover the remaining 55,067 uncovered habitations; 
• Tackle water quality affected habitations to provide safe drinking 
water in a sustainable manner, with priority to tackling problems of 
arsenic, fluoride and salinity; 
• Augment water supply in all habita tions that have siipped back 
from full coverage; 
• To improve the governance of delivery structure for rural water 
supply and sanitation; 
• To increasingly entrust the resp onsibility of rural water supply 
management to local institutions and build their capacity in this 
regard; 
• Provide safe drinking water to all the schools of the country by 
end of 2007; 
• Provide sanitary Toilet facilities to all the schools of the country by 
the end of March 2007; 
• Promote Community/group roof-top rain water harvesting, 
especially in Government buildings, institutional buildings, 
schools, industrial units etc. in rural areas and integrated water 
recharge to augment the water supply for drinking purposes; 
• Move towards enactment of Ground Water Regulations and 
control and development legislation, which could include 
provision for recharging of ground water; 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
• Involve Gram Panchayats/Village Water and Sanitation 
Committees in regular water quality monitoring and 
surveillance; 
• To report all achievement against the targets set on the web-based 
monitoring system on-line; 
• Give more importance to Total Sanitation Campaign to achieve 
the goal of full sanitation by 2012, with full backing for the 
Campaign at the highest political and official level in the State, 
• Make at least one district in each State fully open defecation-free 
by end of 2006; 
• Put Rural India in a place of pride amongst the Nations of the 
World. 
In addition, the following major recommendations were made in the 
Conference: 
1) Total Sanitation Campaign: 
• Increase in unit cost of household and anganwadi toilets and 
inclusion of solid and liquid waste management in the project. 
• Removing community contribution from construction of school 
and anganwadi toilets. 
• A national and state level mass media campaign should be 
launched on Television and Radio for creation of awareness. 
• Population slabs for awarding Nirmal Gram Puraskar should be 
increased. 
2) Implementation of ARWSP in the Eleventh  Plan for 
institutionalization of community participation: 
• Institutionalization of community participation and involvement 
of Gram Panchayats in a phased manner and only one rural water 
supply scheme from the Eleventh Plan. 
• Community contribution of at least 10% of the estimated capital 
cost of the scheme to be an integral part of all rural drinking 
water supply schemes. It may be only 2.5% for SC/ ST habitations. 
The extent of community contribution could be paid in cash, 
labour, land or material or a combination of 
176 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
these. The minimum contribution per household to be decided 
by the State. In difficult single village schemes, quality affected 
habitations, piped water supply from distant sources and multi-
village schemes, the State may decide on quantum of community 
contribution for common facilities. 
• Central and State Governments will bear the balance capital 
cost of approved schemes (after deducting the community 
contribution). In case of difficult single village schemes and 
multi-village schemes, Government agency will bring water 
from the source to the entry point  of the village. The capital 
cost of schemes upto the entry point of habitation will be 
shared by Central and State Government. The distribution 
network of water supply inside the village/habitation will be 
constructed with involvement of the Gram Panchayat/Village 
Water and Sanitation Committees, with community 
contribution and subsequent Operation & Maintenance. They 
will be assisted by PHED in the process. 
3) Coverage and its norms, technology options, source and system 
sustainability, water quality monitoring and surveillance: 
• The distance of the water source should be 0.5 kilometre instead 
of 1.6 kilometre and 30 metres elevation instead of 100 metres in 
hilly areas to lessen the drudgery of carrying water from distant 
source. 
• In hilly areas, the population criteria should be relaxed to cover 
habitations with 50 persons or more or more than 10 households 
to all. 
• There is need for earmarking funds for rooftop/catchment based 
rainwater harvesting and this water may be treated as coverage 
as distinguished from recharging of ground water. 
• Women and youth of rural areas be trained to operate and 
maintain water supply systems. Manuals/guidelines be 
developed for this purpose. 
• Distribution systems be improved for minimizing the leakages. 
States should come up with means to prevent leakages in the 
distribution systems to make it economical with cost recovery. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
• Good production centres/sanitary marts/self-help groups, etc. 
should be utilized for supply of spare parts, training of local 
rural youth and women as mechanics for Operation & 
Maintenance of water sources and also involved in water 
quality monitoring and maintenance. 
4) Some of the States have requested for the funding pattern of 
ARWSP between Center and State to be in the ratio of 75:25 and North Eastern 
States have requested for this ratio to be 90:10 for consideration of the 
Government. 
(d) to (f) Drinking Water Supply is one of the six components of Bharat 
Nirman, which has been conceived as a plan to be implemented in four years, 
from 2005-06 in 2008-09 for building rural infrastructure. The proposed 
coverage in respect of rural drinking  water supply under Bharat Nirman 
(2005-06 to 2008-09) is: 
• Coverage of 55067 uncovered habitations 
• Coverage of water quality aff ected habitations Coverage of 
slipped back habitations based on 2003 survey with priority to 
tackling problems of arsenic, fluoride and salinity. 
• Coverage of slipped back habitations. 
Financial requirement for drinking water component of Bharat Nirman 
during 2005-09: 
• Central Share :   Rs. 25,300 crore 
• State Share :   Rs. 16,336.97 crore 
• Total :   Rs. 41,636.97 crore 
During the 2005-06, the outlay for the Department of Drinking Water 
Supply is Rs. 4,050 crore which is increased to Rs. 4,060 crore. The State/UT 
Governments have reported coverage of 54,890 habitations, including slipped 
back and quality affected habitations till 31.1.2006 against the yearly target 
of 56,270.

Illegal dumping and smuggling of Chinese Silk 
1780. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that illegal dumping and smuggling of cheap 
Chinese silk is affecting the sericulture industry in India; and 
(b) if so, the details and action taken by Government to protect the 
domestic industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) The details of the seizures of 
Cheap Silk smuggled from neighbouring countries are as follows:  
Year No. of cases of seizure of silk yarn/fabrics value (Rs. in crores) 
2002-03 62 5.7133 
2003-04 45 0.7874 
2004-05 32 09.785 
2005-06 13 7.8655 
(upto October, 2005)  
Imports have been liberalized and all restrictions removed. Import duties 
have been lowered to increase imports to meet the demand for silk goods. In 
addition, all units of Directorate of Revenue Intelligence concerned with 
prevention of smuggling are maintaining strict vigil and making all out effort 
to prevent the smuggling of silk. 
Several programmes and schemes to boost the silk industry in the country 
have been instituted. The important ones are: 
1. During the X Plan period, under the Catalytic Development 
Programme, a provision of Rs. 181.00 crores has been made for 
202 

[8 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
providing assistance to sericulture fa rmers/reelers to en courage them to 
adopt improved technology aiming at improvement in quality and 
productivity; 
2. The Central Silk Board (CSB) has evolved new bivoltine breeds with 
assistance from the Japan internatio nal Co-Operation Agency (JICA). The 
commercial exploitation of these breeds has resulted in the production of 
international standard import substitute grade of mulberry raw silk in the 
country; 
3. Through R&D efforts, the CSB has made a break through in 
tropicalising the bivoltine silkworm a nd development of new varieties of 
mulberry plants with higher yields resulting in significant improvement in silk 
productivity; 
4. The SCB has developed improved multi-end reeling units to 
encourage large scale production of international grade quality silk. These 
improved machines are being popularized among the reelers through the 
Catalytic Developmental Programme at important reeling clusters all over the 
country and are producing gradable quality raw silk using the reeling package 
developed by Central Silk Technological Research Institute of Central Silk 
Board; 
5. The CSB is making necessary efforts for the modernization of 
reeling facilities by importing automatic reeling machines to facilitate 
production of international grade quality silk; 
6. The quality of yarn and fabrics in non-mulberry sector has also 
improved considerably through the introduction of motorized silk reeling/ 
spinning machines and setting up of Common Facility Centres. The CSB has 
developed new designs in non-mulberry sector and same are being popularized 
under the brand "Vanya Silk"; 
7. The CSB has launched the "Silk Mark" scheme through the Silk Mark 
Organisation of India (SMOI) which is a hallmark for the products 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2006] 
made from pure natural silk and guarantee the purity of silk products. Silk 
Mark scheme will also play an important role in brand promotion of Indian 
silk in domestic and foreign markets; 
8. The CSB has recently launched futu res trading in cocoon and raw 
silk through National Commodities and Derivatives Exchange Ltd. (NCDEX) 
which, can be effectively used as a t ool to cover the risks associated with 
price fluctuations to boost the production of silk in the country; 
9. Import of raw silk has been liberalized by being brought under OGL, 
which has increased availability of good quality silk enabling the 
manufacturers to produce export quality goods; 
 
10. A number of schemes like Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB), Duty 
Drawback, Duty Free Replenishment Certificate (DFRC) have been made 
available to exporters whereby the element of tax on the exported item is 
reimbursed to them; 
11. Government has rationalized value addition/input-output norms 
specified under the EXIM Policy extended to exporters; 
12. The Government is providing assistance to the Indian Silk Export 
Promotion Council, Mumbai for undertaking various export promotion 
activities such as participation in in ternational fairs, organizing generic 
promotion stalls in domestic fairs like Tex Styles India, Publicity in foreign trade 
magazines, publication of magazine "Silk India" and colour forecast card for 
domestic silk manufacturers, dissemination of overseas trade information 
among exporters, etc; and 
13. For Technological up-gradation of the industry loan at 5% 
point less than applicable rate, under the Technological Up-gradation 
Fund Scheme for the Textiles sector is available inter alia to the silk 
sector;
